whyNot: Amyloid on PET is a **biomarker** of AD pathology found even in cognitively normal elderly and in MCI, so it does not define dementia.
Subjective **memory complaints** are very common in older adults and are part of MCI, so they cannot separate it from dementia.
Age is a risk setting, not a criterion; MCI itself is reported in a sizable share of people over 65.
Testing can document impairment in both conditions; the deciding line is whether **daily function** is significantly affected.
q12-01.why: Dementia is cognitive decline severe enough to interfere with usual daily activities, whereas MCI is only mild decline that does **not yet significantly impair** activities of daily living.

whyNot: Far too low; clinical studies without biomarkers show a yearly conversion several times higher than this.
Too high per year; about **half** of MCI patients meet dementia criteria only after roughly 5 years.
That is roughly the cumulative fraction at **5 years**, not the annual conversion rate.
That is the share proven to have AD after **10 years** or at autopsy, not a yearly rate.
q12-02.why: Without biomarkers, **6–15%** of MCI patients convert to dementia each year, about half by 5 years, and up to 80% prove to have AD by 10 years or autopsy.

whyNot: Aβ plaques are the first of the three autopsy hallmarks of AD, so this option is one of them.
**Tau** tangles are the second hallmark, built from hyperphosphorylated tau.
Substantial neuronal loss, visible to the naked eye at autopsy, is the third hallmark.
An option that does not belong is present, so this fails; **Lewy bodies** are not an AD hallmark.
q12-03.why: AD's three hallmarks are Aβ plaques, tau tangles and neuronal loss; **Lewy bodies** (α-synuclein) define DLB and PDD, though about 30% of AD brains contain them.

whyNot: Sensorimotor and subcortical hypometabolism fits **vascular** dementia, not AD.
AD hypometabolism is described in **posterior cortical** areas; the cerebellum is not the site the book names.
A frontal pattern points to frontotemporal cortices in FTD, not to the posterior pattern of AD.
Parieto-occipital change is listed for Lewy body dementias; AD is **temporo-parietal**, not occipital alone.
q12-04.why: Neuronal loss in AD lowers glucose use mainly in **posterior** regions, especially the temporo-parietal cortex, and the deficit deepens as MCI progresses to dementia.

whyNot: Far too high; vascular dementia is the **second** most common cause, behind AD.
Too low for the second most common dementia, which makes up about a fifth of cases.
Far too small; vascular dementia is a major cause, second only to AD.
Too high; half would make it more common than AD, which is the leading cause.
q12-05.why: Vascular dementia, the **second most common** dementia after AD, accounts for roughly 20% of cases and reflects reduced cerebral blood flow from cerebrovascular disease.

whyNot: Not a vascular finding in the book; MRI there shows white-matter abnormalities and medial temporal atrophy.
Caudate atrophy is tied to PDD pathology, and enlargement is not described for vascular disease.
No pituitary finding is tied to dementia; the vascular marker is **white-matter** disease.
Not a described finding; vascular dementia reflects ischemic damage, white-matter change and microbleeds.
q12-06.why: Vascular dementia reflects reduced cerebral blood flow from small-vessel disease, so MRI shows progressively more **white-matter hyperintensities** as severity increases.

whyNot: **Tau** aggregates into neurofibrillary tangles in AD and some FTLD, not into Lewy bodies.
Huntingtin is not linked to Lewy bodies in the book; they hold α-synuclein.
**Aβ** aggregates into plaques in AD, a separate pathology from Lewy bodies.
TDP-43 is not named; Lewy bodies are built on α-synuclein, with ubiquitin and other proteins mixed in.
q12-07.why: In DLB and PDD, **α-synuclein** misfolds into oligomers and then Lewy bodies and neurites as neurons degenerate, which is why these disorders are called synucleinopathies.

whyNot: This is a **suggestive** feature of DLB, not a core one.
REM sleep behavior disorder is only a **suggestive** feature.
Severe neuroleptic sensitivity is listed as suggestive, not core.
Repeated falls are a **supportive** feature, a lower tier than core.
FTD is defined by early personality and behavior change, not by years of prior motor disease.
Vascular dementia follows cerebrovascular events; the motor-onset timing rule separates DLB from PDD.
**DLB** fits when dementia begins at the same time as, or before, parkinsonism.
AD does not use the motor-onset rule; parkinsonism a year or more before dementia points to PDD.
q12-09.why: When parkinsonian motor symptoms precede dementia by **a year or more**, the diagnosis is PDD; here PD came 4 years earlier. DLB requires dementia first or simultaneously.

whyNot: That is the share with **additional** pathology, especially AD, not the pure proportion.
Too low; roughly one in five has pure LBD pathology.
Far too high given that most LBD patients carry coexisting dementia pathology.
Too high; most patients have mixed pathology, so pure cases are only a fifth.
q12-10.why: Only about **20%** of LBD patients have pure Lewy body pathology; roughly 80% also show other pathology, especially AD, illustrating how common mixed dementia is.

whyNot: Vascular dementia shows slowed processing and impaired abstraction, often after a stroke, not primary personality change.
DLB is marked by fluctuating attention, visual hallucinations and parkinsonism.
Logopenic PPA is a **language** variant; aphasia, not disinhibition, is its presentation.
AD begins with short-term memory loss; this patient's good cued memory argues against it.
q12-11.why: **bvFTD** brings disinhibition, loss of empathy, hyperorality and compulsive behaviors with relatively spared cued memory, unlike the rapid memory loss of AD.

whyNot: Huntington disease is not linked to MAPT in the book, which ties tau gene mutations to FTLD.
MAPT mutations are explicitly **not** associated with AD, where tau acts through tangles instead.
DLB is a synuclein disorder, not a tau-gene disorder.
Vascular dementia stems from impaired blood flow, not tau gene mutations.
q12-12.why: MAPT mutations alter the ratio of 3R to 4R tau, favoring pathological tau accumulation, and are linked to several forms of **FTLD** rather than to AD.

whyNot: Pure vascular pathology is a minority pattern; vascular change usually coexists with other pathology.
Most dementia brains do show pathology, typically several kinds combined.
Single-pathology AD is the exception, not the rule.
Pure Lewy body pathology is uncommon; most LBD patients also have other pathology.
q12-13.why: Postmortem studies show **mixed pathology**, combining protein aggregates and vascular changes, in most dementia patients, which complicates diagnosis and treatment.

whyNot: **β-secretase** makes the first cut in the amyloidogenic pathway, so it promotes Aβ formation.
Acetylcholinesterase breaks down acetylcholine and has no role in APP processing.
Choline acetyltransferase **synthesizes** acetylcholine; it does not cut APP.
**γ-secretase** completes the amyloidogenic pathway, producing Aβ peptides of 38–43 residues.
q12-14.why: **α-secretase** cleaves APP within the Aβ region (non-amyloidogenic pathway), so no intact Aβ forms; β- then γ-secretase cutting generates Aβ instead.

whyNot: Aβ42 is **more aggregation-prone** and toxic, but it is less common than Aβ40.
Not an isoform the book lists; γ-secretase yields peptides of 38 to 43 amino acids.
Aβ38 sits at the short end of the 38–43 range and is not the most common.
Aβ43 is **rare**, though thought to aggregate even more readily than Aβ42.
q12-15.why: γ-secretase yields Aβ peptides of 38–43 amino acids; **Aβ40** predominates, whereas Aβ42 aggregates more readily and is regarded as more toxic.

whyNot: Opposite direction: the protective allele is APOE2, whereas APOE4 raises risk.
An understatement; even a single APOE4 copy gives a larger increase than this.
That is the risk increase with **one** copy of APOE4, not two.
Overstated; two APOE4 copies raise risk by an amount well short of this.
q12-16.why: APOE4 raises risk in a dose-dependent way: one copy gives about threefold and **two copies about tenfold**, making APOE a prominent genetic influence in AD.

whyNot: APOE3, the most common form, confers **intermediate** risk between APOE2 and APOE4.
APOE1 is not an allele discussed; the forms named are APOE2, APOE3 and APOE4.
**APOE4** raises AD risk, threefold with one copy and tenfold with two.
One allele does appear protective, so this is wrong; APOE2 offers some protection.
q12-17.why: **APOE2** appears protective, APOE3 (the most common allele) confers intermediate risk, and APOE4 raises risk.

whyNot: That is the **skeptics'** view, that Aβ merely marks neuronal death, not the proponents' defense.
High placebo response is raised about D2-blocker trials, not as the amyloid proponents' explanation.
Proponents note that many drugs did **successfully engage** Aβ targets yet showed no benefit.
Isoform choice is not the argument; the defense concerns when treatment starts.
q12-18.why: Anti-Aβ trials enrolled patients with MCI or overt AD; proponents argue the cascade is by then **self-perpetuating** with irreversible damage, so treatment must precede symptoms.

whyNot: Opposite direction: CSF Aβ is **reduced** because Aβ is held in the brain.
CSF Aβ is already **abnormal** at this stage, falling as amyloid deposits.
Elevated CSF tau signals neurodegeneration in stage 2, and Aβ is low rather than elevated.
Aβ is reduced, not absent; the change is a fall in CSF levels.
q12-19.why: In asymptomatic amyloidosis, Aβ is deposited in the brain rather than cleared into CSF, so CSF Aβ is **low** while amyloid PET turns positive.

whyNot: Not all; the figure shows more than half only in the 80–90 age band.
Some are Aβ-negative, but about a quarter are positive, so this understates.
Far above the real figure; only about a quarter of normal elderly are positive.
About 5% matches the youngest age band in the figure, not elderly controls overall.
q12-20.why: Roughly **a quarter** of cognitively normal elderly people are Aβ-positive on PET and are considered to have presymptomatic AD despite having no symptoms.

whyNot: Low CSF Aβ reflects **amyloidosis**, Aβ being held in the brain.
Amyloid PET labels Aβ plaques directly, so it is an amyloidosis marker.
APOE4 is a genetic risk factor, not a measure of neurodegeneration.
Aβ40 is simply the commonest isoform; it is not a neurodegeneration marker in the book.
q12-21.why: Neurodegeneration is shown by **elevated CSF tau** (also NfL, MRI atrophy and FDG PET hypometabolism), whereas amyloid PET and low CSF Aβ mark amyloidosis.

whyNot: Too low; roughly half of MCI patients lack Aβ deposition.
Too high; the other half do show moderate or severe Aβ deposition.
Not none; a substantial share of MCI patients are Aβ-negative.
Not all; about half have moderate or severe Aβ deposition.
q12-22.why: About **half** of MCI patients have no Aβ on imaging, so their cognitive symptoms probably stem from another cause, such as depression or a different dementia-causing disorder.

whyNot: **α-secretase** acts on APP processing, which is amyloid biology, not tau's effect on synapses.
Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase is a **drug** mechanism that raises ACh, not what tau does.
Microglia play no role in the book's account of tau and synaptic dysfunction.
NMDA blockade describes **memantine**, not hyperphosphorylated tau.
q12-23.why: Hyperphosphorylated tau can no longer bind and stabilize **microtubules**, so vesicle transport to the synapse fails and synapses malfunction; tau also forms tangles.

whyNot: Tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting step for **catecholamine** (dopamine) synthesis, not ACh.
Glutamic acid decarboxylase makes **GABA** from glutamate, not acetylcholine.
Butyrylcholinesterase **breaks down** ACh rather than making it.
Acetylcholinesterase **terminates** ACh action by breaking it down; it does not synthesize it.
q12-24.why: Choline acetyltransferase (**ChAT**) combines choline with acetyl coenzyme A, which neurons make from glucose in mitochondria, to produce acetylcholine.

whyNot: Purkinje cells are not named; BuChE is described in glia, with AChE concentrated in neurons receiving ACh.
AChE, not BuChE, is concentrated in neurons that receive ACh input.
Dopamine neurons are not a BuChE site in the book; glia are.
Synaptic vesicles store ACh via VAChT; they are not where BuChE sits.
q12-25.why: In the brain BuChE sits mainly in **glial cells**, whereas AChE is abundant in neurons receiving ACh input; BuChE activity rises with gliosis as cortical neurons die.

whyNot: M3 and M5 are **excitatory** postsynaptic receptors, not autoreceptors.
M1 and M3 are excitatory postsynaptic; M1 is the memory-related subtype.
M1 and M5 are excitatory postsynaptic receptors, so they do not curb ACh release.
M1 is an **excitatory** postsynaptic receptor important for memory, not an autoreceptor.
q12-26.why: **M2 and M4** are inhibitory presynaptic autoreceptors that curb further ACh release once it builds up, whereas M1, M3 and M5 are excitatory postsynaptic receptors.

whyNot: α3β4 is not a subtype the chapter discusses; the key brain subtypes are α7 and α4β2.
Muscle-type nicotinic receptors lie **outside the brain**, in skeletal muscle and ganglia.
M4 is a **muscarinic** receptor, and it restrains mesolimbic dopamine rather than regulating accumbens release the nicotinic way.
α7 receptors facilitate ACh release and support prefrontal cognition rather than being nicotine's main target here.
q12-27.why: The **α4β2** nicotinic subtype is postsynaptic, regulates dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens, and is a main target of nicotine, linking it to tobacco's reinforcing effects.

whyNot: ACh breakdown is done by the enzymes AChE and BuChE, not by α7 receptors.
On glutamate neurons, α7 receptors **facilitate** glutamate release, not inhibit it.
Choline reuptake is handled by the choline transporter, not α7 receptors.
Opposite direction: inhibition of ACh release is the job of M2/M4 autoreceptors; α7 facilitates.
Raphe neurons are the **serotonin** source in the book, not the memory-related cholinergic projection.
The tuberomammillary nucleus is the **histamine** source involved in wakefulness.
The locus coeruleus supplies **norepinephrine** to the cortex, not the memory-related ACh pathway.
The substantia nigra supplies **dopamine** to the striatum, not these cholinergic projections.
q12-29.why: Cholinergic neurons of the basal forebrain project to the prefrontal cortex, amygdala and hippocampus and are thought especially important for memory; their early loss drives memory decline.

whyNot: Cholinesterase inhibitors are **symptomatic** and do not remove amyloid or halt neurodegeneration.
They block ACh breakdown rather than increasing the synthetic enzyme ChAT.
NMDA blockade describes **memantine**, a different mechanism from cholinesterase inhibition.
They cannot regenerate neurons; they only boost ACh at the surviving targets.
q12-30.why: Early in AD the presynaptic cholinergic input is lost but **postsynaptic targets survive**, so slowing ACh breakdown restores some function, much as levodopa does in Parkinson's.

whyNot: Not discussed in the book; the chapter's cholinesterase inhibitors are donepezil, rivastigmine and galantamine.
Galantamine adds nicotinic positive allosteric modulation to AChE inhibition.
Not discussed in the book as an AD drug; the chapter's inhibitors are donepezil, rivastigmine and galantamine.
Rivastigmine is **pseudoirreversible**, intermediate-acting, and also inhibits BuChE.
q12-31.why: **Donepezil** is a reversible, long-acting inhibitor selective for AChE without BuChE inhibition; it is easy to dose, and its mostly GI side effects tend to be transient.

whyNot: Memantine is an **NMDA** antagonist, not a cholinesterase inhibitor.
Galantamine inhibits AChE and also modulates nicotinic receptors; BuChE inhibition is not its signature.
Donepezil is **reversible** and selective for AChE, sparing BuChE.
Not discussed in the book; the chapter's cholinesterase inhibitors are donepezil, rivastigmine and galantamine.
q12-32.why: **Rivastigmine** is pseudoirreversible (reversing over hours) and inhibits both AChE and BuChE, including glial BuChE; a transdermal patch greatly reduces its GI side effects.

whyNot: 5HT2A antagonism belongs to agents like pimavanserin and brexpiprazole, not galantamine.
BuChE inhibition is a feature of **rivastigmine**, which is pseudoirreversible.
M1 agonism is described for xanomeline, not galantamine.
NMDA channel blockade is the mechanism of **memantine**.
q12-33.why: Galantamine is also a **positive allosteric modulator** at nicotinic receptors, a second action that could theoretically boost ACh effects, though a clinical advantage is unproven.

whyNot: The book ties side effects to peripheral AChE blockade in the **gut**; kidney is not named.
The retina is not named; the peripheral effect described is gastrointestinal.
Liver is not the source of the common side effects; GI cholinergic effects are.
Skin is not a site; the transdermal rivastigmine patch avoids peripheral GI effects.
q12-34.why: Cholinesterase inhibitors also block AChE in the periphery, and the resulting boost of ACh in the **gastrointestinal** tract causes the typical, often transient GI side effects.

whyNot: AMPA receptors only help depolarize neurons; memantine acts on the NMDA channel itself.
Glycine is a cotransmitter needed to open the channel; memantine is a pore blocker, not an agonist.
Memantine has **low** affinity, unlike PCP and ketamine, which block much more powerfully.
It is **uncompetitive**, plugging the channel when open, not competing at the glutamate site.
q12-35.why: Memantine plugs the open NMDA channel at the magnesium site with low affinity, voltage dependence and fast on-off kinetics, blocking tonic glutamate leak but not phasic bursts.

whyNot: Memantine is a channel blocker, not a glycine-site agonist.
It acts on NMDA receptors, not AMPA receptors.
It acts like **artificial magnesium** at the same channel site; it is not metabolized into magnesium.
It does reach the brain, where it acts on NMDA receptors in Alzheimer disease.
q12-36.why: Because memantine binds with low affinity and fast kinetics, a phasic glutamate burst with depolarization expels it from the channel, behaving like **artificial magnesium** without PCP-like effects.

whyNot: A year is far longer than the criterion, which requires only **one month**.
Three months exceeds the stated duration criterion.
Six months exceeds the stated duration criterion.
One week is too short; the definition requires persistence of at least a **month**.
q12-37.why: Dementia-related psychosis means delusions or hallucinations arising after cognitive decline, lasting **at least one month** and not better explained by delirium or another mental illness.

whyNot: Memantine targets cognition and has not been systematically tested for agitation.
Benzodiazepines are among the agents the book does not favor, and sedatives raise aspiration pneumonia risk.
Cholinesterase inhibitors give little behavioral benefit except in Lewy body dementias.
D2 blockers carry a boxed warning and are used only cautiously after weighing risks, not as a first step.
q12-38.why: Before drugs, manage reversible precipitants such as pain, nicotine withdrawal, medication side effects, illness and provocative environments, and use **non-drug** approaches first.

whyNot: Agranulocytosis is not the dementia warning; the boxed warning concerns cardiovascular events.
Hepatic failure is not the warning cited; it is stroke and death.
Seizures are not the cited warning; the concern is cardiovascular events and mortality.
Hyponatremia is not the cited warning; it is stroke and death.
q12-39.why: D2 blockers carry a black-box warning in elderly dementia because they raise **stroke and mortality**, via stroke, thromboembolism, falls, QT effects and aspiration pneumonia.

whyNot: AD hallucination prevalence is only about 11–17%, far below DLB.
MCI is not dementia and does not appear in the psychosis prevalence table.
FTD has the lowest psychosis prevalence of the dementias listed.
Vascular dementia hallucinations are only about 5–14%.
q12-40.why: DLB has the highest hallucination prevalence (**55–78%**), mostly visual, with Parkinson's disease dementia next at 32–63%.

whyNot: The common delusions described are paranoid and misidentification types, not grandiose.
Visual hallucinations typify the **Lewy body** dementias, not AD, where delusions predominate.
Auditory command hallucinations are not the AD pattern described.
Tactile hallucinations are a minority feature in PD psychosis, not the usual AD form.
q12-41.why: In AD, delusions outnumber hallucinations and are most often **persecutory** (theft, infidelity) or misidentification, whereas visual hallucinations typify the Lewy body dementias.

whyNot: The psychosis network involves excess downstream **dopamine** activity, not low striatal dopamine.
Acetylcholine in the thalamus is not part of the model; the problem is glutamate and 5HT2A drive.
Cerebellar degeneration is not part of the psychosis network.
The problem is excitatory **5HT2A** stimulation, not 5HT1A overstimulation.
q12-42.why: Loss of GABA interneurons leaves 5HT2A-driven glutamate output unchecked, and excess glutamate release in the **visual cortex** is hypothesized to produce visual hallucinations.

whyNot: Mania is not an approval the book lists; pimavanserin is approved for Parkinson's disease psychosis.
Only positive trials in dementia-related psychosis of all causes are described; approval is for PD psychosis.
Alzheimer psychosis is not an approved use in the book; pimavanserin is approved for PD psychosis.
Pimavanserin's approved use here is PD psychosis; schizophrenia is covered by D2-based agents.
q12-43.why: Pimavanserin, a selective **5HT2A antagonist**, is approved for Parkinson's disease psychosis; for dementia-related psychosis of all causes, the book cites only positive trials.

whyNot: Thalamic output is what the filter **restricts**; top-down inhibition is not driven by thalamus to cortex.
The hippocampus-to-amygdala link is not part of the thalamic-filter model.
Locus coeruleus to cortex is a **bottom-up** norepinephrine arousal output of the amygdala.
Amygdala to VTA is a bottom-up limbic route that releases dopamine and worsens the filter.
q12-44.why: Cortical glutamate neurons release glutamate in the **striatum**, which drives GABA release onto the thalamus and filters sensory and emotional input; loss of this brake produces agitation.

whyNot: H1 antagonism is not among the five actions the book lists for brexpiprazole.
M1 antagonism is not among brexpiprazole's listed actions in this model.
Brexpiprazole is not a reuptake inhibitor; SSRIs and SNRIs are a separate approach.
NMDA antagonism is the mechanism of **dextromethorphan**, not brexpiprazole.
q12-45.why: Beyond D2 and 5HT1A partial agonism and 5HT2A antagonism, brexpiprazole blocks **α1 and α2** adrenergic receptors, dampening locus coeruleus norepinephrine arousal on pyramidal dendrites.

whyNot: D2 partial agonism belongs to **brexpiprazole**, not dextromethorphan–bupropion.
5HT2A antagonism is how pimavanserin and brexpiprazole act, not this combination.
GABA-A modulation is not described for this combination.
Cholinesterase inhibitors give little behavioral benefit outside Lewy body dementias.
q12-46.why: Dextromethorphan's **NMDA antagonism** is thought to quell the excess glutamate output of the agitation network, while bupropion adds NDRI action and inhibits CYP450 2D6.

whyNot: Gabapentin is mentioned as a possible second-line option, not one to avoid.
Carbamazepine has shown perhaps the best efficacy among unapproved agents, though with risks.
SSRIs and SNRIs are considered first-line pharmacological options by many experts.
β blockers are listed among second-line options.
q12-47.why: The book places **benzodiazepines** (along with valproate, topiramate and oxcarbazepine) among agents not to use for agitation, and sedatives also raise aspiration pneumonia risk.

whyNot: Far too large; the increase is about double.
Opposite direction: MDD history raises risk rather than lowering it.
Not true; a history of MDD is linked to higher dementia risk, especially vascular.
Tenfold matches APOE4 homozygosity, not depression history.
q12-48.why: A history of major depression doubles dementia risk, particularly vascular dementia, and depression with late-life onset may be a prodromal sign of AD.

whyNot: Weight gain is not raised in the book as the citalopram–escitalopram difference.
Hepatotoxicity is not the cited difference between the two.
Hyperprolactinemia is not the cited difference between the two.
Agranulocytosis is not the cited difference between the two.
q12-49.why: Citalopram prolongs the QT interval, whereas escitalopram may offer similar efficacy without that problem, an important consideration in elderly dementia patients.

whyNot: Lithium is not discussed for PBA; the book names dextromethorphan with quinidine.
Memantine is used for cognition in AD, not approved for PBA.
Pimavanserin is for PD psychosis, not emotional expression disorders.
Donepezil is a cholinesterase inhibitor for memory, not for PBA.
q12-50.why: Dextromethorphan with quinidine treats PBA, presumably through NMDA glutamate and σ receptor actions; quinidine is the CYP450 2D6 inhibitor in the combination.

whyNot: The cerebellum is not part of the ABC model of apathy.
The occipital cortex is not part of the ABC model.
DLPFC dysfunction underlies **cognitive** apathy, not affective apathy.
Motor areas and DMPFC underlie **behavioral** apathy, not affective apathy.
q12-51.why: In the ABC model, **affective apathy** (emotional blunting, altered social interaction) is tied to ventromedial prefrontal and orbitofrontal dysfunction; behavioral involves motor areas and DMPFC, cognitive the DLPFC.

whyNot: Pain can drive behavior problems, but the book does not trace apathy to pain.
Apathy does not resolve spontaneously; it is among the most persistent symptoms.
Excess serotonin is not the cause; dopaminergic and cholinergic systems are implicated.
Dopamine agonists, not D2 blockers, are among the suggested options.
q12-52.why: Apathy is a disorder of **motivation**, not depression: guilt, worthlessness and hopelessness are typically absent, so antidepressants have little target to act on.

whyNot: Agranulocytosis is not a warning the book attaches to dementia drugs; its boxed warning is stroke and death with D2 blockers.
QT prolongation is raised for citalopram and D2 blockers, not as the issue for anti-amyloid antibodies.
Serotonin syndrome is not tied to anti-amyloid antibodies.
Hepatic failure is not tied to anti-amyloid antibodies in the book.
q12-53.why: Anti-amyloid antibodies can cause **ARIA**, brain edema or microbleeds, and risk is higher in APOE4 carriers; the book lists these antibodies only as a disease-modifying approach.
